title: Three men and a stranger
told: a story the Prophet ﷺ told

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there something you have that you know was given to you, not earned?
options: keep it in mind. this story is about remembering.
fair. listen, and see what you think after.

steps.line: The Prophet ﷺ told of three poor men, long ago: one with a skin disease people shrank from, one bald, and one blind.
God sent an angel to test them. Each was healed, and given one animal about to give birth: a camel, a cow, a sheep.
Years passed. The first had a valley full of camels, the second a valley of cows, the third a valley of sheep.

steps.q: The angel came back to each, looking as that man once had, a poor stranded traveler, asking for just one animal. What do you think happened?
steps.why: Two refused. One remembered. The story is in Bukhari and Muslim.

steps.line: The first two said no. “I have many costs,” they said, and “I inherited all this.” They had forgotten where it came from.
The third said: “I was blind, and God gave me back my sight. Take whatever you want.” “Keep it,” the angel said. “You were only being tested.”

steps.q: Why could the third man give so easily?
o: He remembered it had been given to him
He was richer than the other two
He guessed the stranger was an angel
steps.why: He never forgot he’d been given it. The other two told themselves it was all theirs.

steps.line: That’s the heart of zakat. Its root, z-k-w, means both to purify and to grow. Like pruning a vine: cut some away, and what’s left grows better.

steps.q: The Qur’an calls the needy’s share “a known right” in wealth. What does that make zakat?
o: A kindness, left up to the giver
A debt already owed to the poor
A gift that earns the giver praise
steps.why: Surah 70 speaks of “a known right” in wealth for those who ask and those in need. Given that way, the giver is paying what’s owed, not doing a favor.

steps.line: Today, once a year, a Muslim with savings above a set line, the nisab, gives two and a half percent. Often worked out at a kitchen table, with a pencil.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Zakat has a set share. Its cousin, sadaqa, is giving of any kind. How small can sadaqa get, in the Prophet’s ﷺ words?
o: Nothing less than a day’s bread
At least one coin, given in secret
Even a smile at your brother
steps.why: “Your smile in the face of your brother is charity,” says a hadith in Tirmidhi. Moving a stone off the road counts too.

say: here’s what i love. the third man’s answer starts with memory: “i was blind.” he gives because he remembers.
in islam, zakat is a pillar: a share of savings given each year to people in need. the qur’an calls it a known right in wealth, already theirs, handed back.

steps.q: The two who refused both said, in effect, “this is all mine.” From this lesson, why might zakat be called a purification?
o: It cleans money that was earned wrongly
It loosens the grip of “all mine”
It makes the giver look generous
steps.why: The Qur’an says charity purifies those who give (9:103). It cleans the heart first: each year you remember what the third man remembered. Money gained wrongly isn’t cleaned by zakat; it has to be given back.

today.say: today, try the third man’s memory. name one thing you have that was given to you, a skill, a home, someone’s help, and pass a small share of it on: a donation, a meal, an hour. if you’re curious, try a zakat calculator, just to see how it works.
options: lovely. the third man would smile.
good. it’s simpler than it sounds.

tomorrow.line: a sacred stone, a cloak with four corners, and a whole city that trusted one man.

card.from: a story the Prophet ﷺ told
card.keepWhy: What you give purifies what you keep.
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3464; Sahih Muslim 2964 (three men of the Children of Israel, one with a skin disease (abras), one bald, one blind; an angel healed each and gave a pregnant she-camel, cow and ewe; later came in the man’s former likeness as a poor traveler; the first two refused (“the rights are many”; “I inherited this”); the blind man said “take what you will”; “you were only tested; Allah is pleased with you”)
Qur’an 9:103 (take alms of their wealth to purify them)
Qur’an 70:24-25 (in whose wealth there is a known right for the beggar and the destitute)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1454 (Abu Bakr’s letter: on silver, a quarter of a tenth)
Jami‘ at-Tirmidhi 1956 (your smile in your brother’s face is charity)
Root z-k-w (purity, growth): Lane, An Arabic-English Lexicon
check: The story itself is about gratitude and giving generally; the lesson links it to zakat. Nisab and 2.5% are simplified; Shia khums is not mentioned. Confirm.
